screens.title: Raising Custom Exceptions and Assertions
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll learn how to signal problems in Python using the raise statement, how to design custom exception classes that carry useful context, and when to use assert as a development-time sanity check. You'll see concrete code examples that show raising built-in exceptions like ValueError, writing a custom InsufficientFundsError that stores balance details, and building an update_stock function for an inventory where domain-specific exceptions make error handling clearer. We'll also draw a firm distinction between raise, which you use for expected runtime issues and user or business errors, and assert, which you should reserve for internal invariants that help you find bugs while developing. By the end of the lesson you'll know how to create exception classes that inherit from Exception or a more specific subclass, how to raise them with helpful messages and attributes, and why assertions can be disabled in optimized runs so they should not be used for production input validation. A short hands-on task walks through implementing ProductNotFoundError and InvalidQuantityError and testing them with try-except. Keep an eye out for the common mistake of using assert as validation — we'll explain why that can silently break your checks when optimization is enabled.

screens.title: Raising built-in exceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Raising a built-in exception is a direct way to tell calling code that something went wrong. The typical pattern is to validate input and, when a condition fails, raise an exception like ValueError or TypeError with a descriptive message. For example, if a function requires a non-negative age, you can raise ValueError with a short message explaining why. This moves error handling to the caller, which can decide whether to retry, log, or abort. A common misconception is that exceptions are only for catastrophic failures: in fact, they are a normal control flow tool for signaling contract violations. Another mistake is using vague messages; instead include enough context to debug quickly. Here is a compact code example that demonstrates raising and catching a ValueError. The example prints a friendly error message when validation fails, showing how to surface the original explanation for debugging or user feedback. When you write library code, prefer typed exceptions over printed errors — they are machine-handled and composable. Practice creating descriptive messages, and remember that raising an exception is not the end of responsibility; design your A P I’s documentation and callers to handle the expected exception types.

keyIdea.title: When to raise
keyIdea.text: Raise built-in exceptions to enforce preconditions and push handling to the caller with a clear message.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Raise built-in exceptions
Code example
# Validate and raise a built-in exception for bad input
def set_age(age):
  if not isinstance(age, int):
    raise TypeError("age must be an integer")
  if age < 0:
    raise ValueError("Age cannot be negative")
  return age

# Caller handles the exception
try:
  print(set_age(-5))
except (TypeError, ValueError) as e:
  print("Validation error:", e)
Why this helps
  • Signals contract violations explicitly so callers can respond.
  • Provides standard exception types that are recognizable across codebases.
  • Preserves stack traces and message context for debugging and logging.
Example scenario

A library that accepts configuration should raise clear exceptions if a required field is missing or of the wrong type so application code can fall back or show a helpful error to users.

Key Takeaway

Use raise with built-in exceptions and descriptive messages to enforce input contracts and let callers decide recovery.

screens.title: Separation of detection and handling
screens.narratorSegment: A clean design principle is to separate error detection from error handling. A function that detects an invalid condition should raise an exception rather than handle user interaction or logging itself. This keeps the function focused on its core responsibility and allows different callers to decide what to do: retry, log, wrap, or present a message. A common pattern is validation at the top of a function followed by raise when validation fails, then documented exception types so callers know what to catch. An important misconception to avoid is coupling recovery logic to the low-level function — this reduces reuse and forces duplication. For example, a library function should raise FileNotFoundError when a file is missing; the application code can choose whether to attempt a fallback path or show an error to the user. When you document your functions, list the exceptions that they raise and under what conditions. This process is also essential for automated testing: tests assert that the correct exceptions are raised for invalid inputs. Ultimately, raising keeps behavior predictable and gives calling code the flexibility to implement context-specific recovery strategies.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Separation of detection and handling
Steps
  1. Validate inputs or state at the start of a function.
  2. If a condition fails, raise a meaningful exception with context.
  3. Document which exceptions a function may raise.
  4. Let callers decide how to recover — retry, default, or abort.
This makes your code easier to reuse and test; unit tests can assert that the correct exception type is raised for invalid inputs.
Concrete example

A file parser raises FileNotFoundError when the path is invalid. An application using the parser can choose to prompt the user for a new path, log the error, or abort processing.

Common mistake

Do not swallow errors inside low-level functions by printing and returning None. That hides failure modes and forces brittle caller logic.

Pro tip

Document exceptions in your docstrings so callers can write focused except blocks.

screens.title: Custom exception classes
screens.narratorSegment: Custom exceptions are user-defined classes that inherit from Exception or one of its subclasses. They let your code express domain-specific problems with names and attributes that are meaningful to your application. By convention, names end with Error, for example InsufficientFundsError. A custom exception can store values such as balance and amount, so exception handlers can inspect those attributes without parsing a message string. Always call super(). init(message) so the base Exception behavior and message are preserved. A useful pattern is to include a short docstring explaining why the exception exists and what attributes it exposes. One misconception is that custom exceptions are heavy or unnecessary; in fact, when used appropriately they make except blocks precise and simplify recovery logic. Another good practice is to inherit from a relevant built-in subclass when it makes semantic sense; for example, inheriting from ValueError signals that the problem relates to an invalid value. Below is a class example demonstrating these ideas, followed by a brief note on naming and documentation. Custom exception classes means create named exception classes with attributes and a message; call super to preserve base behavior and document what the class represents.. In practical terms, define exceptions that express your domain and carry context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Custom exception classes
Example class
class InsufficientFundsError(Exception):
  """Raised when an account withdrawal exceeds the available balance."""
  def __init__(self, balance, amount):
    self.balance = balance
    self.amount = amount
    self.message = f"Attempted to withdraw {amount} with only {balance} available."
    super().__init__(self.message)
Why include attributes?

Handlers can read balance and amount directly, enabling context-aware recovery, such as suggesting a transfer or partial withdrawal.

Naming convention

End class names with Error and pick a base class that reflects the kind of error, like ValueError for invalid values.

Key Takeaway

Custom exception classes improve clarity and make except blocks precise and maintainable.

screens.title: Inheriting from specific exception subclasses
screens.narratorSegment: When designing a custom exception, consider inheriting from a specific subclass of Exception rather than Exception itself if it clarifies the nature of the problem. For instance, inheriting from ValueError signals that the error relates to an invalid value, while inheriting from IOError or OSError might make sense for file or network-related failures. This semantic inheritance helps library users catch groups of related errors with a single except clause. It also keeps your exception hierarchy expressive: you can create a base domain error and derive several specific errors from it. A common misconception is that picking Exception is simpler; over time, however, that broadness makes catch-all except blocks more likely and reduces the opportunity for targeted recovery. The architecture pattern is to create a small hierarchy: a top-level DomainError and child classes for specific cases. This supports both general and specific handling strategies. Document your inheritance choices so callers understand what broader categories your exceptions belong to. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Inheriting from subclasses
Small hierarchy pattern
Create a domain root, then derive specific errors. This allows callers to catch DomainError to handle all related failures, or catch a specific child to react differently. 
class InventoryError(Exception):
  pass

class ProductNotFoundError(InventoryError):
  def __init__(self, product_id):
    self.product_id = product_id
    super().__init__(f"Product '{product_id}' not found")
Why it helps
  • Enables broad or narrow except blocks.
  • Makes intent explicit to library users.
  • Supports structured logging and error categorization.
Misconception check

Avoid overly deep hierarchies unless your domain requires nuanced handling; start simple and extend as needed.

Pro tip

Pick a meaningful base class and document the exception family in your library docs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Inventory update_stock
Starter code
class ProductNotFoundError(Exception):
  """Raised when a product ID is not found in the inventory."""
  def __init__(self, product_id):
    self.product_id = product_id
    super().__init__(f"Product with ID '{product_id}' not found.")

class InvalidQuantityError(ValueError):
  def __init__(self, message):
    super().__init__(message)

inventory = {"P101": 50, "P102": 120, "P103": 30}

def update_stock(product_id, quantity_change):
  if product_id not in inventory:
    raise ProductNotFoundError(product_id)
  if not isinstance(quantity_change, int) or quantity_change == 0:
    raise InvalidQuantityError("Quantity change must be a non-zero integer.")
  new_stock = inventory[product_id] + quantity_change
  if new_stock < 0:
    raise InvalidQuantityError(f"Cannot reduce stock below zero for '{product_id}'. Current: {inventory[product_id]}, Attempted change: {quantity_change}")
  inventory[product_id] = new_stock
  return new_stock
Test scenarios
  1. Valid update increments stock.
  2. Missing product raises ProductNotFoundError.
  3. Non-integer quantity raises InvalidQuantityError.
  4. Negative resulting stock raises InvalidQuantityError.
  5. Zero quantity raises InvalidQuantityError.
Key Takeaway

Domain-specific exceptions make your API easier to test and reason about; they allow callers to react with context-aware logic.

screens.title: The assert statement
screens.narratorSegment: The assert statement evaluates a condition and raises AssertionError with an optional message when the condition is false. Its primary role is to catch bugs early by validating internal invariants — conditions that should always be true if your code is correct. For example, you might assert that a computed final_price is non-negative after a discount calculation. A crucial property to remember is that assertions can be disabled when Python runs with the optimize flag. Because of this they are not suitable for runtime validation of external input or security checks. def calculate_discount(price, discount_rate):

Pattern

def check_age(age):

Step 2 — Custom exception
class InvalidCredentialsError(Exception):
  def __init__(self, username, reason):
    self.username = username
    self.reason = reason
    super().__init__(f"Invalid credentials for {username}: {reason}")

def login(user, password):
  # Simulated check
  if user != 'admin' or password != 'secret':
    raise InvalidCredentialsError(user, "invalid username or password")
Step 3 — Assert for dev checks

  assert len(token) > 0, "token must not be empty"
  # Further processing assuming token exists

In this chapter we'll learn how to signal problems in Python using the raise statement, how to design custom exception classes that carry useful context, and when to use assert as a development-time sanity check. You'll see concrete code examples that show raising built-in exceptions like ValueError, writing a custom InsufficientFundsError that stores balance details, and building an update_stock function for an inventory where domain-specific exceptions make error handling clearer. We'll also draw a firm distinction between raise, which you use for expected runtime issues and user or business errors, and assert, which you should reserve for internal invariants that help you find bugs while developing. By the end of the lesson you'll know how to create exception classes that inherit from Exception or a more specific subclass, how to raise them with helpful messages and attributes, and why assertions can be disabled in optimized runs so they should not be used for production input validation. A short hands-on task walks through implementing ProductNotFoundError and InvalidQuantityError and testing them with try-except. Keep an eye out for the common mistake of using assert as validation — we'll explain why that can silently break your checks when optimization is enabled.

Over the next screens you'll learn practical skills for signaling and diagnosing errors in Python. First, you'll practice explicitly raising built-in exceptions, so you can stop execution when input or state violates required conditions. Second, you'll design custom exception classes and attach contextual attributes to them, which helps calling code make informed recovery or logging decisions. Third, you'll implement the inventory update example that demonstrates how to raise domain-specific errors like ProductNotFoundError and InvalidQuantityError and how to document their behavior. Fourth, you'll understand how and when to use assert for development-time invariant checks, and why assertions should not replace runtime validation.
